Amberjack Greater.Description:
Found around wrecks, reefs, and rocky outcrops, typically in 60 to 300 feet of water, though juveniles may be found near the surface.

Opportunistic feeders eating squid, crustaceans, and fish.

Ballyhoo.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Ballyhoo.Conditions: No species-specific recreational size/season rule is listed on the current FWC recreational index. Area-specific and bait-gear restrictions can still apply.
Ballyhoo.Gear: Use recreational gear legal for the location and target method.
Ballyhoo.Description:
Young are found in open waters.

Adults found in bays and nearshore waters close to reefs.

Barracuda Great.MaxSize: 36 in slot; one fish >36 in/person or vessel
Barracuda Great.Description:
Range inshore to offshore.

Young found inshore in seagrass beds. Top predator in reef areas, consuming fishes, squid and shrimp.

Bass Black Sea.Description:
They are found in the coastal waters near structure and rocky bottoms.

Smaller specimens are often found inshore in finger channels. Up to 24 inches (8 pounds), common to 12 inches (1.5 pounds)

Bermuda Chub.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Bermuda Chub.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Bermuda Chub.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Bermuda Chub.Description:
They are found in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans, inhabiting shallow coastal areas, rocky bottoms, and coral reefs.

Young chubs are often found among floating sargassum seaweed.

Blue Fish.BagLimit: 3/person/day in Nassau–Miami-Dade state waters; federal private 3/person, for-hire 5/person
Blue Fish.Description:
(May contain elevated mercury levels) - Opportunistic predators that feed on a wide range of prey, including squid, menhaden, and smaller fish.

Found in temperate to warm waters in the western Atlantic and other oceans. They are pelagic (open ocean) schooling fish that migrate seasonally, moving north in the spring and south in the fall.

Bone Fish.Gear: Hook and line only; multiple hooks prohibited.
Bone Fish.Description:
They feed on bottom-dwelling invertebrates such as clams, snails, crabs, and shrimp, using their specialized mouth to forage in sand and mud.

Lives in shallow coastal waters, intertidal flats, mangrove areas, and river mouths. They are found in tropical and subtropical waters worldwide, including the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans.

Bonito.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Bonito.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Bonito.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Bonito.Description:
They are pelagic, schooling fish found from Nova Scotia to Florida and the Gulf of America in the West, and from Norway to South Africa in the East.

They are highly active predators that feed on small fish, such as anchovies and sardines, as well as squid.

Butterfly Fish Banded.BagLimit: Marine-life aggregate: 20 organisms/person/day; max 5 of one species
Butterfly Fish Banded.Conditions: Marine-life harvest rules require organisms to be landed alive with adequate aeration/oxygenation. Recreational sale is prohibited.
Butterfly Fish Banded.Gear: Hand collection, hand-held net, drop net, barrier net or slurp gun as allowed by FWC marine-life rules.
Butterfly Fish Banded.Description:
Omnivorous foragers that eat reef-dwelling invertebrates such as polychaete worms, coral polyps, and anemones.

Found in shallow-water coral reefs and rocky areas, primarily the tropical western Atlantic Ocean, including the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of America, and the coasts of Florida, Bermuda, and New England.

Butterfly Fish Foureye.BagLimit: Marine-life aggregate: 20 organisms/person/day; max 5 of one species
Butterfly Fish Foureye.Conditions: These limits are for live marine-life/aquarium collection; food harvest and protected areas may differ.
Butterfly Fish Foureye.Gear: Only legal marine-life collection gear; collection is restricted/prohibited in protected areas.
Butterfly Fish Foureye.Description:
They are carnivores that use their pointed mouths to feed on small invertebrates, such as worms, coral polyps, and gorgonians.

Usually found in shallow coral reefs, rocky reefs, and seagrass beds at depths of 6–65 feet (2–20 m) in Western Atlantic Ocean, from Massachusetts to Brazil, including the Gulf of America and the Caribbean.

Butterfly Fish Reef.BagLimit: Marine-life aggregate: 20 organisms/person/day; max 5 of one species
Butterfly Fish Reef.Conditions: These limits are for live marine-life/aquarium collection; food harvest and protected areas may differ.
Butterfly Fish Reef.Gear: Only legal marine-life collection gear; collection is restricted/prohibited in protected areas.
Butterfly Fish Reef.Description:
They are carnivorous or omnivorous, primarily eating invertebrates like coral polyps, anemones, worms, and crustaceans.

Some species also consume algae. Lives in shallow coral reefs, with some species also found in seagrass beds or near brackish water bays.

Cobia.Gear: Hook and line, spear, gig, seine or cast net.
Cobia.Description:
Found in both inshore and nearshore waters, often near natural and manmade structures like reefs, wrecks, buoys, and pilings.

Found in both inshore and nearshore waters, often near natural and manmade structures like reefs, wrecks, buoys, and pilings.

Croaker Atlantic.Description:
Opportunistic bottom feeders, they eat worms, crustaceans (like shrimp and crabs), and small fish.

Found over sandy or muddy bottoms in coastal waters, estuaries, and bays. Young fish are typically in estuaries, while older fish move to deeper offshore waters in the winter.

Dog Snapper.Description:
Solitary, nocturnal carnivores found in coastal waters, reefs, and rocky areas at depths of 5–100+ meters.

Massachusetts to Brazil, including the Caribbean and Gulf of America. Primarily feeds on fishes, crustaceans, and invertebrates.

Dolphinfish.Description:
Hunts small fish (like flying fish), crabs, and other small marine life.

Lives near the surface in warm, tropical/subtropical waters worldwide, often schooling as juveniles and alone as adults.

Drum Black.Gear: Hook and line, cast net, seine, spear or gig. No snatching or multiple hooks with natural bait.
Drum Black.Description:
Bottom-feeders that use their chin barbels to find and their strong throat teeth to crush prey like clams, oysters, crabs, worms, and other shellfish.

Coastal bays, sounds, inlets, and river mouths, and can be found around oyster beds, docks, and bridge pilings.

Drum Red.Description:
Bottom feeders that prey on crabs, shrimp, and small fish.

Found in coastal and estuarine waters from Massachusetts to Key West, Florida, and along the entire Gulf coast to northern Mexico.

Drum Spotted.BagLimit: Marine-life aggregate: 20 organisms/person/day; max 5 of one species
Drum Spotted.Conditions: Marine-life/aquarium collection rule; protected-area restrictions apply.
Drum Spotted.Description:
Also known as the (Spotted Ribbonfish) is a Nocturnal feeder.

At night, it leaves its shelter to feed on small crustaceans (like shrimp and crabs) and polychaete worms found in the substrate. It primarily inhabits coral reefs, in shallow lagoons, reef faces, and near pier pilings.

Flounder Gulf.Gear: Hook and line, spear, gig, seine or cast net. No snatching or multiple hooks with natural bait.
Flounder Gulf.Description:
Caught with various methods, including hook and line, jigs, and gigging, especially at night in shallow waters.

Inhabits sandy or muddy bottoms in coastal waters, bays, and tidal creeks. Juveniles are often found in higher salinity seagrass beds.

Flounder Peacock Atlantic.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Flounder Peacock Atlantic.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Flounder Peacock Atlantic.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Flounder Peacock Atlantic.Description:
Peacock flounder is a distinct flatfish species and is not one of the four flounders covered by Florida’s species-specific flounder closure.

Inhabits sandy or muddy bottoms in coastal waters, bays, and tidal creeks. Juveniles are often found in higher salinity seagrass beds.

GoatFish Yellow Saddle.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
GoatFish Yellow Saddle.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
GoatFish Yellow Saddle.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
GoatFish Yellow Saddle.Description:
Yellow goatfish with a yellow lateral stripe and yellow tail; often schools over reef-adjacent sand.

Tropical reefs, rubble and sandy flats.

GoatFish Yellowstripe.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
GoatFish Yellowstripe.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
GoatFish Yellowstripe.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
GoatFish Yellowstripe.Description:
Yellowstripe goatfish is an Indo-Pacific goatfish occasionally encountered outside its native range; verify identification carefully.

Warm reef and sandy-bottom habitats.

Goatfish Spotted.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Goatfish Spotted.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Goatfish Spotted.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Goatfish Spotted.Description:
Spotted goatfish is a western Atlantic goatfish with dark body markings and chin barbels.

Reefs, seagrass edges and adjacent sand.

Grouper Black.Seasons: State: year-round; federal seaward of 20 fathoms closed Feb 1–Mar 31; The Edges closed Jan 1–Apr 30
Grouper Black.Description:
Primarily eats fish, squid and crustaceans.

Adults prefer rocky bottoms, reefs, and drop-off walls, while juveniles can be found in seagrass beds and oyster rubble. Usually found in the Western Atlantic, from Massachusetts to Brazil, including the Gulf of America and the Caribbean.

Grouper Coney.Description:
Primarily eats small reef fish, crustaceans, crabs, and shrimp.

Found in reef areas, seagrass beds, and around caves and crevices.

Grouper Gag.Description:
Adults primarily eat a variety of fish, crabs, shrimp, and squid.

Juvenile gag groupers, less than 8 inches, feed on crustaceans in shallow seagrass beds. Adults are typically found on rocky reefs and other hard-bottom habitats from coastal waters down to 500 feet.

Grouper Goliath.BagLimit: Harvest prohibited without an FWC Goliath Harvest Program permit
Grouper Goliath.Conditions: Do not harvest unless holding the required limited-entry permit and complying with permit terms.
Grouper Goliath.Description:
Found in coastal and nearshore waters, often near natural and man-made structures like bridges, docks, and artificial reefs.

They also inhabit estuaries, especially around mangroves.

Grouper Graysby.Description:
Primarily eats small reef fish, crustaceans, crabs, and shrimp.

Found in reef areas, seagrass beds, and around caves and crevices.

Grouper Nassau.Description:
(If you accidentally catch one, you must release it immediately and handle it with care.) They eat crustaceans and smaller fish.

Juveniles eat crustaceans and bivalves, while larger adults feed on fish, lobsters, and gastropods. Their range is limited to south Florida and the Florida Keys, with their presence on the Gulf side being rare.

Grouper Snowy.Description:
The snowy grouper (Hyporthodus niveatus) is a highly prized deep-water reef fish known for its firm, mildly sweet, white meat.

Found in the western Atlantic, these ambush predators live on rocky bottoms and steep ledges, typically at depths of 200 to 1,200 feet. As top ambush predators, they eat fish, squids, and crustaceans.

Grouper Tiger.Description:
Carnivorous, eating smaller fish, crabs, shrimp, and octopus.

Solitary ambush predator, using camouflage to surprise prey like fish, crabs, and squid. Found in warm, clear waters of Western Atlantic reefs, from Florida to Brazil; adults prefer deeper reefs, juveniles use seagrass beds.

Grouper Yellowfin.Seasons: State: year-round; federal seaward of 20 fathoms closed Feb 1–Mar 31; The Edges closed Jan 1–Apr 30
Grouper Yellowfin.Description:
Adults prefer rocky/coral reefs and ledges; juveniles live in seagrass beds and mangroves.

Carnivorous, eating smaller fish and cephalopods. Known to carry ciguatera toxin, so caution is needed when eating.

Grunt Bluestriped.Conditions: No species-specific statewide recreational size/season rule. Biscayne National Park has stricter minimum sizes for these grunts.
Grunt Bluestriped.Gear: Standard recreational gear where otherwise legal.
Grunt Bluestriped.Description:
Nocturnal carnivore, eating shrimp, crabs, mollusks, small fish, and worms.

Found in coastal to offshore, favoring reefs, seagrass, sand flats, and hard bottoms from Virginia to Brazil, Gulf of America, Caribbean Sea

Grunt Porkfish.BagLimit: Marine-life aggregate: 20 organisms/person/day; max 5 of one species
Grunt Porkfish.Conditions: Marine-life/aquarium collection rule; protected-area restrictions apply.
Grunt Porkfish.Description:
Primarily nocturnal predators of invertebrates, such as mollusks, crustaceans, and worms.

Found in shallow waters, from 6 to 65 feet deep, over reefs and rocky bottoms. Juveniles are often found in seagrass beds.

Grunt White.Conditions: No species-specific statewide recreational size/season rule. Biscayne National Park has stricter minimum sizes for these grunts.
Grunt White.Gear: Standard recreational gear where otherwise legal.
Grunt White.Description:
Nocturnal carnivore, eating shrimp, crabs, mollusks, small fish, and worms.

Found in coastal to offshore, favoring reefs, seagrass, sand flats, and hard bottoms from Virginia to Brazil, Gulf of America, Caribbean Sea

Gulf Kingcroaker.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Gulf Kingcroaker.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Gulf Kingcroaker.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Gulf Kingcroaker.Description:
Found in coastal waters, common in surf zones along beaches.

Feeds on fishes and invertabrates.

Hogfish.Conditions: Gulf rule applies north of Cape Sable; special Biscayne National Park rules can supersede the general rule.
Hogfish.Gear: Spears, gigs, hook and line, seine or cast net where legal; reef-fish gear requirements apply.
Hogfish.Description:
hey inhabit offshore reefs, hard-bottom areas, and rocky ledges, typically in 10-100 feet of water, feeding on mollusks and crustaceans.

They use their snouts to dig in the sand for crabs, sea urchins, and mollusks. They are often found in small groups or harems, with one male protecting multiple females.

Jack Blue Runner.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Jack Blue Runner.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Jack Blue Runner.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Jack Blue Runner.Description:
Adults feed on fish, shrimp and squid.

Juveniles found offshore. Adults found inshore and nearshore.

Jack Crevalle.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Jack Crevalle.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Jack Crevalle.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Jack Crevalle.Description:
Feeds on smaller fish, shrimp, and invertebrates and is known for being a powerful fighter.

Found in a variety of environments, including offshore waters, reefs, seagrass beds, and estuaries. They can also move into brackish and even freshwater tributaries.

Jack Yellow.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Jack Yellow.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Jack Yellow.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Jack Yellow.Description:
Found in the Gulf of America, the Caribbean, and along the Florida Atlantic coast.

They inhabit deep wrecks in summer and shallow reefs/flats in winter. Eats live shrimp on a yellow jig head is the top choice.

Ladyfish.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Ladyfish.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Ladyfish.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Ladyfish.Description:
Lives in tropical and subtropical coastal waters, including the Atlantic seaboard and Gulf of America.

Usually found inshore, brackish waters, bays, estuaries, mangrove areas, and even completely fresh water. Feeds from small fish and crustaceans (especially shrimp).

Mackerel Cero.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Mackerel Cero.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Mackerel Cero.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Mackerel Cero.Description:
Common in clear, tropical/subtropical waters, especially around coral reefs, wrecks, and structure from New England to Brazil, but most abundant in the Florida Keys and Caribbean.

Eats small schooling fish (sardines, herring) and squid.

Mackerel King.Description:
Found in coastal or open ocean waters, migrates seasonally with water temperatures.

Opportunistic carnivores, eating menhaden, mullet, herring, sardines, squid, and shrimp.

Mackerel Spanish Atlantic.Gear: Beach/haul seine, cast net, hook and line, or spear.
Mackerel Spanish Atlantic.Description:
Migrates along the U.S.

Atlantic Coast from Florida (winter) north to New York/New England (summer) and into the Gulf of America. Forms large, fast-moving schools near the surface in coastal waters, barrier islands, and passes.

Mullet.Conditions: More restrictive seasonal bag limits apply in portions of Pinellas County; seasonal night closures apply in portions of Charlotte County. License exception: FWC states mullet may be taken from fresh water with a freshwater fishing license; species-specific mullet harvest limits still apply. Special lake, river, Fish Management Area, protected-species, emergency-order, and access rules can be more restrictive; verify the selected waterbody before harvest.
Mullet.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, seine or cast net. Spearfishing mullet in fresh water is prohibited.
Mullet.Description:
Found worldwide in tropical and temperate seas, often near shores, estuaries, and even freshwater, swimming in schools.

Primarily eat algae, detritus (decaying organic matter), phytoplankton, and zooplankton.

Needle Fish.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Needle Fish.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Needle Fish.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Needle Fish.Description:
Primarily eats small fish.

Younger fish that have not yet developed a full (beak) eat plankton. Primarily found in shallow, coastal marine waters, bays, and estuaries, but some species can also be found in freshwater rivers and canals.

Palometa.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Palometa.Conditions: General Florida unregulated-species recreational limit; park/sanctuary restrictions can still apply.
Palometa.Description:
The palometa (Trachinotus goodei), also commonly known as the great pompano, is a sleek, silver marine game fish of the jack family found in the western Atlantic Ocean, from Massachusetts to Argentina, the Caribbean, and the Gulf of America.

Their diet primarily consists of small crustaceans (like mole shrimp and crabs), marine worms, mollusks, and smaller fish

Permit.Gear: State: hook and line only. Federal: hook and line or spear.
Permit.Description:
Found in shallow, warm inshore waters like flats, channels, and near reefs in the Western Atlantic, especially abundant in South Florida and the Caribbean.

Opportunistic feeders, using their crushing teeth to eat crabs, mollusks, and sea urchins, often digging in the seafloor. The Special Permit Zone includes state and adjacent federal waters south of a line running due east from Cape Florida in the Atlantic at 25° 40 North Latitude, waters of Biscayne Bay south of Rickenbacker Causeway, and south of a line just south of Cape Sable running due west through federal water

Pinfish.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Pinfish.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Pinfish.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Pinfish.Description:
Found in the Western Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of America, on seagrass beds, coral reefs, rocky bottoms, and estuaries; juveniles prefer shallow water.

Daytime feeder omnivorous species, eating algae, seagrass, plankton, small crabs, shrimp, and mollusks. Considered an excellent, underrated panfish, similar to other porgies or snapper.

Pinfish Spottail.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Pinfish Spottail.Conditions: No species-specific FWC size/season rule. Area-specific closures and standard recreational gear rules still apply.
Pinfish Spottail.Gear: Hook and line, spears, gigs, haul seines and cast nets where otherwise legal.
Pinfish Spottail.Description:
Found in the Western Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of America, on seagrass beds, coral reefs, rocky bottoms, and estuaries; juveniles prefer shallow water.

Daytime feeder omnivorous species, eating algae, seagrass, plankton, small crabs, shrimp, and mollusks. Considered an excellent, underrated panfish, similar to other porgies or snapper.

Pompano African.Gear: State: hook and line only. Federal: hook and line or spear.
Pompano African.Description:
Found in tropical and subtropical seas worldwide, including the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans.

Prefers coastal waters, reefs, and wrecks, often in depths from near the surface to deeper waters. Feeds on crabs, shrimp, and small fish; they are known to prefer live food.

Pompano Florida.Gear: Hook and line, cast net, beach or haul seine; no snatching/multiple natural-bait hooks.
Pompano Florida.Description:
Eats small clams, sand fleas, and other small invertebrates.

Prefers sandy surf flats and nearshore areas. Found along the Atlantic coast from Massachusetts to Brazil, with high concentrations near Florida.

Porgy Red.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Porgy Red.Gear: Hook and line, spears or gigs; reef-fish gear requirements apply.
Porgy Red.Description:
Found in rocky or sandy bottoms, typically at depths of 90 to 350 feet on the continental shelf.

Carnivorous, feeding on crustaceans (crabs, shrimp), mollusks (snails, clams), sea urchins, worms, and small fish.

Seatrout Spotted.Conditions: One over 19 in allowed per vessel, or per shore angler. Captain/crew may not retain on for-hire trips.
Seatrout Spotted.Gear: Hook and line or cast net; no snatching/multiple natural-bait hooks.
Seatrout Spotted.Description:
Commonly found in shallow, inshore waters, tidal creeks, and seagrass beds (often 4–10 feet deep) from New York to Mexico, with high concentrations in the Gulf of America.

They prefer water temperatures between and moving to deeper, warmer waters during. Primarily diet shrimp, pinfish, pigfish, and mullet and/or small crustaceans.

Shark Bull.Conditions: Shark must be landed whole; shore-based shark fishing permit/course requirements apply.
Shark Bull.Gear: Hook and line only; non-offset non-stainless circle hooks with natural bait.
Shark Bull.Description:
Bull sharks are opportunistic feeders with a wide diet that includes fish, seals, birds, dolphins, sea turtles, and other sharks.

Found in warm, coastal waters worldwide, they are one of the few sharks that can tolerate freshwater and are often found in rivers and estuaries. (Shore-based anglers: You must take and pass the Shore-Based Shark Fishing Course online and carry the free permit with you at all times.

Sheepshead.Gear: Hook and line, cast net, seine, spear or gig; no snatching/multiple natural-bait hooks.
Sheepshead.Description:
Found near piers, pilings, jetties, reefs, and oyster beds in coastal waters.

Carnivores eating crustaceans, mollusks (crabs, oysters, clams) using powerful jaws. Use light tackle and be quick to set the hook; chumming with crushed shells helps.

Snapper Black.Description:
Adults are found over sandy or rocky bottoms, often near the continental shelf edge, while juveniles occupy shallower, inshore waters.

Opportunistic predators feeding on small fishes, shrimp, worms, and squid.

Snapper Blackfin.Description:
Adults are found on deep rocky ledges and sandy bottoms near the edge of the continental shelf.

Primarily feeds on smaller fish.

Snapper Cubera.BagLimit: 10/person within aggregate; max 2 fish over 30 in per person/vessel
Snapper Cubera.Description:
Powerful predators of fish and large crustaceans, using their strong jaws.

Adults prefer offshore rocky ledges, wrecks, and reefs; juveniles live inshore in seagrass beds and mangroves. Can exceed 120 pounds and reach over 5 feet long, though commonly around 40 pounds.

Snapper Gray Mangrove.Description:
Found in the Indian and Western Pacific Oceans.

Juveniles often live in mangrove-lined estuaries, moving to deep, offshore reefs and wrecks as they mature. They are opportunistic carnivores that feed on small fish, crustaceans (shrimp, crabs), and cephalopods, particularly at night.

Snapper Lane.Description:
Found in inshore over seagrass beds as juveniles, moving to deeper coral reefs and structures as adults.

Usually under 14 inches, but can grow larger. Feeds from shrimp, squid, cut bait, and minnows work well.

Snapper Mahogany.Description:
Adults live in clear, shallow waters around coral reefs, mangroves, and rocky bottoms.

They form large, tight schools during the day, often mixed with other snapper species like grunts. Nocturnal predators that eat small fish, shrimp, crabs, and cephalopods.

Snapper Mutton.Description:
Opportunistic predators eating crustaceans (shrimp, crabs), mollusks, small fish, and squid.

Active day and night, picking prey from surfaces, and adopting darker, barred patterns when feeding near the bottom. Found in the Western Atlantic, from Massachusetts to Brazil, common in Florida, the Caribbean, and Gulf of America.

Snapper Queen.Description:
They prefer rocky, deep-sea habitats and are often found in the Caribbean, Gulf of America, and near the Bahamas.

Queen snapper primarily feed on small fish, squid, and crustaceans.

Snapper Red.Seasons: 2026: May 22–Jul 31; Sep 1–Oct 4 plus listed fall/holiday weekends through Jan 4, 2027
Snapper Red.Conditions: Private-vessel and qualifying non-federally-permitted charter season; check current FWC page for exact fall dates.
Snapper Red.Description:
Found in the Gulf of America and along the Atlantic coast, preferring offshore structures like reefs, wrecks, and oil rigs.

Carnivores, eating fish, shrimp, crabs, squid, and worms.

Snapper Schoolmaster.Description:
Found in the Indian and Western Pacific Oceans.

Juveniles often live in mangrove-lined estuaries, moving to deep, offshore reefs and wrecks as they mature. They are opportunistic carnivores that feed on small fish, crustaceans (shrimp, crabs), and cephalopods, particularly at night.

Snapper Vermilion.Description:
Found in waters 60-400 feet deep, often over reefs, rocks, and sand.

Offshore, from North Carolina to Brazil, in the Gulf of America. Adults form large schools near structures.

Snapper Yellowtail.Description:
Invertebrates (shrimp, crabs, worms) and small fish, also plankton.

Forms large schools, especially juveniles in seagrass; adults near reefs, often above the bottom. Coastal reefs in the Western Atlantic, from Massachusetts to Brazil, especially abundant in the Caribbean and Florida Keys.

Snook Common.Conditions: Snook permit + recreational fishing license required; keep whole; no captain/crew retention.
Snook Common.Description:
Found in coastal waters, estuaries, mangroves, and sometimes freshwater, particularly in Florida and the Gulf of America.

Highly euryhaline, allowing them to thrive in both saltwater and freshwater, often moving between them for spawning. Opportunistic predators that feed on fish, crabs, and shrimp.

Tarpon.BagLimit: Catch and release; one tag/year only when pursuing a state/IGFA record
Tarpon.Conditions: Tarpon over 40 in must remain in the water except when a tag authorizes record pursuit.
Tarpon.Gear: Hook and line only; special Boca Grande restrictions apply.
Tarpon.Description:
While they live in coastal, saltwater environments, they can tolerate varying salinity, including freshwater.

They are carnivorous, feeding on fish, crabs, and shrimp.

Tilefish Blueline.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Tilefish Blueline.Description:
Tilefish inhabit the outer continental shelf and upper continental slope along the entire east coast of the United States and the Gulf of America south to Venezuela.

They are found in waters from 250-1,500 feet deep, where bottom temperatures range from 49° to 58° F. Individuals live in cone-shaped burrows, and concentrate in small groups or pods.

Tilefish Golden.BagLimit: 2 fish or 100 lb/person/day, whichever is greater
Tilefish Golden.Description:
Tilefish inhabit the outer continental shelf and upper continental slope along the entire east coast of the United States and the Gulf of America south to Venezuela.

They are found in waters from 250-1,500 feet deep, where bottom temperatures range from 49° to 58° F. Individuals live in cone-shaped burrows, and concentrate in small groups or pods.
